newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus expected to fall slowly in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus expected to fall slowly in 1997/98.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus will continue to shrink next fiscal year, but the pace of the decline will slow due to the effect of the weaker yen, leading economists predicted in a Reuters poll released on Thursday.

Predictions of 24 economists from banks, brokerages and research institutes, produced an average forecast of a surplus of 6.5 trillion yen ($57.5 billion) in the year from April 1997. This was less than an average forecast of 7.1 trillion yen ($62.8 billion) in a previous survey in July.
"The basic trend is that the surplus will continue to shrink on the back of globalisation of Japanese industries," said Hisashi Yamada, an economist at the Japan Research Institute.

"However, the hike in the consumption tax will slow down the economy next fiscal year and the trend of a weaker yen seems to be established. Taking these factors into account, the tempo of decline in the surplus is likely to slow down."
The consumption tax is due to increase from three percent to five percent on April 1.
The survey covered economists at 30 institutions, who were polled between October 15 and October 17. Not all responded to all the questions.
The 23 forecasts received for the merchandise trade surplus figure produced an average of 8.1 trillion yen ($71.6 billion), down from July's average estimate of 9.2 trillion yen ($81.4 billion).
For this fiscal year, economists predicted a current account surplus of 7 trillion yen ($61.9 billion) and a merchandise trade surplus of 8.6 trillion yen ($76.1 billion).
Japan's actual current account surplus last fiscal year was 9.48 trillion yen ($83.8 billion), while its trade surplus was 9.13 trillion yen ($80.7 billion).

Despite a more than 40 percent rebound in the dollar's value against the yen since last April, Japanese manufacturers have continued to move production bases overseas to avoid high costs at home, respondents to the survey said.

This phenomenon has reduced exports from Japan and increased imports as companies ship back products made abroad for sale to domestic consumers. The situation has also helped push up income from investments made overseas, one component of the current account data.

The yen hit a record high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995, accelerating Japanese companies' restructuring efforts and shifts of production bases abroad. But since then, the currency has slipped and it was trading at around 112.80 to the dollar on Thursday.

Survey respondents said the dollar's rebound against the yen had slowed down a flood of cheap imports, giving domestic producers some breathing space. The increase in the consumption tax should also dampen domestic demand, they said.

The dollar's strength had given some support to exports, but the effect was likely to be limited as major exporters, such as car and electronics firms, had already moved many production bases abroad, they said.

Respondents said the deficit in services trade, the other component of the current account, may shrink due to a decline in the numbers of Japanese travelling overseas resulting from the yen's fall, but again, the effect was expected to be limited.
The rise in global oil prices, meanwhile, could push up imports, but many saw this as a temporary factor.
A small number of respondents predicted that the surplus would start rising again in 1997.
"The fall in trade surplus should bottom out by early next year and then, start rebounding," said Tomoko Fujii, an economist at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd. ($1=113 yen)
